questions.prompt: What is the correct order of service worker lifecycle events on a fresh registration?

options.label: fetch → install → activate
install → activate → fetch
register → fetch → install → activate
install → fetch → activate (fetch fires during install)

questions.explanation: After registration, the SW transitions: install → (possibly waiting) → activate → fetch. `fetch` events only fire on the active SW; you can't intercept requests during install. If a previous SW is controlling clients, the new one waits between install and activate unless `skipWaiting` + `clients.claim` are used.

options.label: Return cache; only fetch network if cache is missing
Try network first; fall back to cache on failure
Return cache immediately, fetch network in parallel, update cache for next time
Wait for both network and cache, return whichever finishes first

questions.explanation: SWR is the workhorse strategy. Cache hits return instantly; the network request runs in parallel and updates the cache for the next visit. The user sees yesterday's data now, today's data on next reload. The price: a moment of UI inconsistency if the network response differs visibly from the cache.

questions.prompt: Why call `self.clients.claim()` inside the activate event?

options.label: It registers the SW with the browser's update tracker
It allows the new SW to take control of pages that are already open, without waiting for navigation
It claims the cache namespace so other SWs can't write to it
It's required by the spec for a SW to start handling fetch events

questions.explanation: By default, even after a SW activates, pages that loaded under the previous SW stay attached to it until the user navigates. `clients.claim()` overrides that — the new SW takes over immediately. Combined with `skipWaiting()` in install, you get instant updates. Combined with nothing, you can sit waiting all day.

questions.prompt: What's the production reality of the Background Sync API?

options.label: Works everywhere; just register a sync tag
Works in all major browsers except Safari on iOS
Chromium-only — Safari and Firefox don't ship it, so you must build an app-level IndexedDB queue as the floor and use SW sync as an optimization
Removed from the spec — use Periodic Sync instead

questions.explanation: Background Sync has been Chromium-only since 2016 and shows no sign of changing. The production pattern is an IndexedDB outbox that drains on the `online` event (works everywhere), with an optional `registration.sync.register()` layer for Chromium users that drains even when no tab is open.

questions.prompt: Why does the browser require HTTPS for service worker registration?

options.label: Performance — HTTPS connections are faster than HTTP, and SWs need fast startup
Spec compatibility — old SW polyfills only worked on HTTPS
Because a SW is a programmable proxy with persistent control over an origin's requests; HTTPS prevents a network attacker from injecting a malicious SW that owns your origin
Cache size — HTTPS storage has a higher quota than HTTP

questions.explanation: A SW can intercept every request from your origin and persist past the tab closing. On plain HTTP, a MITM could inject JavaScript that registers a malicious SW that takes permanent control of your origin in the user's browser. HTTPS prevents the injection. `localhost` is the one exception because there's no meaningful MITM in the loopback case.
